items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: He was from Boston and one of the finest students Schlossberg had.

ctx.x: Yes. We were just talking about that section that he was in.

Yes. He was from Boston and one of the finest students Schlossberg had. And his ambition was to play in the Boston Pops because he was from Boston. But he ended up with Noble Sissle. He couldn’t get a job. They didn’t hire black musicians in symphony bands in those days. So we all ended up doing one-nighters. You know we’d pass each other on the road going to Birmingham or Texas or Mississippi. We played every nook and corner in the United States.

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I never had an Auburn, from Herbert Clarke or from Schlossberg. None of those books that taught you how to…you still had to have somebody teach you how to read.

ctx.x: Before we get too far into Count Basie, one question before we leave your early background: you said your uncle had taught you the scales, the trumpet. How did you actually learn to read music, was that from him as well, or…?

Well, it takes a professional to really teach you the finer points of music, how to read the dynamics in music. He wasn’t that equipped because he had never been formally trained himself. But he taught me the scales and he used to send and get John Philip Sousa’s books of marching and I never had an Auburn, from Herbert Clarke or from Schlossberg. None of those books that taught you how to…you still had to have somebody teach you how to read. But he taught me how to read the scales, how to read the chromatic…
Did you have any formal musical training?
